title: The water footprint of data centers: cooling, indirect use and trade-offs

sources.title: Data Centers and Water: Frequently Asked Questions (R49057, July 31, 2026)
sources.note: 報告引用 LBNL 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report 與 IEA Energy and AI（2025）的估計

sources.title: AI programs consume large volumes of scarce water (2023-04-28)

facts.text: A data center is a building or facility that houses and runs large computer systems; its processors and other equipment produce heat that must be removed to keep the systems working.
Many larger data centers use cooling towers, in which part of the water evaporates and carries heat away into the air.
Water consumption means water taken from a source that is not returned to it, mainly because it has evaporated.
Cooling water can be reused on site several times, but evaporation leaves dissolved minerals behind; when they become too concentrated, the water has to be discharged.
Data centers that rely on evaporative cooling need more water during the hotter parts of the day and the hotter seasons of the year.
Data centers also use water indirectly, because many power plants that supply their electricity use cooling towers that evaporate water.
The International Energy Agency estimates that about 40 percent of data centers' water use happens on site and about 60 percent happens at power plants.
One study estimated that U.S. data centers directly used about 17 billion gallons of water in 2023, compared with 5.6 billion gallons in 2014.
Derived from f8: 17 billion gallons is about 3 times (3.04 times) the 5.6 billion gallons used in 2014, an increase of about 11.4 billion gallons.
Air-cooled chillers use no water, but they use more energy than cooling systems based on evaporation.
UC Riverside researchers estimated that training the AI model GPT-3, which took about two weeks, in Microsoft's U.S. data centers consumed about 700,000 liters of fresh water.
Unlike web searches or video streaming, AI training can be scheduled for almost any time, so it could be moved to cooler hours when less water evaporates.
Scheduling for cooler hours can conflict with scheduling for low carbon emissions, which favors running when solar power is plentiful.
Direct water use by data centers makes up about 2 percent of total U.S. water consumption, but it can strain the water supply of individual communities.
